entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Aelius Paetus Catus was a Roman Republican consul elected in 198 BC, whose interpretation of the laws of the Twelve Tables is known primarily through Cicero's praise. Born into a prominent plebeian noble family, Paetus Catus came from an influential clan with a long history of producing notable figures in Roman politics.

A member of the equestrian order, Paetus Catus served as consul alongside his brother Publius Aelius Paetus, who also held consular office. The Paetii family played a significant role in shaping Rome's early government, with their ancestors serving as prominent magistrates and holding influential positions within the Roman Republic.

Praetorian Prefect Gaius Cornelius Lentulus Gauntius is known to have served under Paetus Catus during his consulship. Paetus Catus' contribution to Roman law was instrumental in shaping the city's governance, with his interpretation of the Twelve Tables having a lasting impact on Roman jurisprudence.

Sextus Aelius Paetus Catus' legacy extends beyond his role as a Roman consul, as he represents an important chapter in the development of Rome's political and legal systems. His influence can be seen in the enduring legacy of the Twelve Tables, which continued to shape Roman law for centuries to come.

Through his service as consul, Paetus Catus demonstrates the significant impact that individual leaders can have on shaping the course of history, leaving a lasting legacy that continues to inform our understanding of ancient Rome's governance and legal systems.
